newsitem.title: UK: Analysts see gold price staying low in '97 - poll.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see gold price staying low in '97 - poll.

text.p: Gold prices are likely to remain under $400 per ounce next year and will peak in the first six months of the year, according to a narrow majority of analysts polled by Reuters.
A stock market fall was widely forecast to help prices but low inflation and the threat of central bank and producer selling would limit gold market reaction, many analysts said.

Only Rhona O'Connell at London-based stock broker T. Hoare and Co saw gold at $400 by the end of next year by which time Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) analyst Andy Smith had the yellow metal around its lowest of the year at $340.
Average gold prices forecast for 1997 varied from $360 (Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch and Jason Wong of Po Sang bank) to $390 (O'Connell and Greg Drury of Mitsui Bussan).
On the basis of New York's nearby Comex contract, CPM group forecast gold peaking in the fourth quarter at $416 and averaging $405 for the year.
Several analysts expected funds to switch investments from overheating stock markets to gold next year but the counter would be continuing fears of official sales.

Makoto Tonoki at Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo KK forecast a rebound in gold demand in Asia "will also help gold prices rebound slightly. But any price gains would be capped by talk of the IMF's gold sales plan".

Mitsui Bussan's San Francisco-based analyst Greg Drury placed his 1997 high of $420 at end second quarter citing increased nervousness towards stock market valuations and followed by a stock market correction in the second quarter.
But he added, "Producer selling and central bank selling in response to a price rally will stop gold/silver going above historical highs."
However UBS's Smith saw confirmation of a central bank sale could bring being complete relief to the market.

"A New Year move up in gold could be triggered by an announcement of central bank sales, portfolio shuffle from securities into metal or postponement of EMU (and relief of immediate official selling paranoia)," he said.
But longer term Smith saw the price being at risk from producers, physical buyers standing off and (above all) "more mobile" central banks.
T. Hoare's O'Connell warned, "An equity market meltdown could change everything."

Paul Gooday at AME Mineral Economic in Sydney reckoned demand from the jewellery sector provided a floor at around $370 but "any move towards $390 or above would see strong producer forward selling thus bringing the price back down".
There was only a little more optimism for the white metals which were not under threat from institutional selling or being demonetised.
Spot silver was seen averaging between 475 cents (Arnold) and 550 cents (Drury) next year with most analysts seeing the highs in the first half.
Spot platinum looked set to average under $400 next year with only Drury seeing an average above that ($410) while only UBS's Smith saw palladium getting as high as $130.

Tonoki said "Gains in platinum group metals could be limited...global platinum demand for autocatalysts will be sluggish on increased use of palladium rich autocatalysts. Palladium demand would be pressured by a drop in Japan's electronic sector."

Weaker Japanese palladium demand would cap any price rise based on concerns over Russian stocks (of platinum especially) and the delay in Japan-Russia year end talks for 1997 contracts, according to Nissho Iwai Corp's Jun Ohaguro.

Swiss Bank's Hanspeter Hausheer said of the white metals, "As they are fundamentally industrial metals, they should profit from the economic recovery in the industrial countries...in contrast to gold there are no big potential sellers looming over the silver market."
